sections.synopsis: A low pressure system will descend from British Columbia tonight into Sunday, bringing precipitation to Western Washington. Conditions look to remain cooler and unsettled next week as additional systems move through the area.
sections.short_term:
High clouds starting to stream overhead across Western Washington early this morning. Temperatures continue to drop as well, with the latest observations showing temperatures in the low 30s to low 40s. A frontal system associated associated with a low pressure system just off the coast of British Columbia will move south into Western Washington this evening. Light precipitation is expected with this system, with rain reaching the coastline this evening and then filling into the interior by Sunday morning. The bulk of the precipitation is expected along the coast and the Olympics. The parent upper level low is expected to continue its southward track Sunday into Monday. The majority of models favor the center of the low pressure system moving into Oregon, which should render drier conditions for the region. However, shall center of the low track more towards the Oregon/Washington border, it may keep light showers in the forecast for Monday.

High temperatures in the mid to upper 50s. Low temperatures in the in the low 30s to low 40s increasing to the upper 30s to mid 40s by Monday.
sections.long_term: Conditions look to remain generally unsettled into Friday. There is general agreement among ensemble guidance a broad upper level trough will remain situated over the region Tuesday with a low pressure system to the north. Models are now trending wetter on Wednesday and Thursday, as the low pressure system moves southward. Cooler temperatures expected next week, with the coldest temperatures expected late in the week; high temperatures in the low to mid 50s and low temperatures in the low 30s to low 40s.
sections.marine: A surface low southwest of Haida Gwaii will shift southward today into tonight and an associated occluded front will clip the coastal waters on Sunday morning. Increasing easterly or southeasterly gradients will lead to small craft advisory winds across the coastal waters as well as the Strait of Juan de Fuca. Seas will build to 10 to 12 feet over the coastal waters late today into Sunday. The surface low is expected to move onshore over northwest Oregon Sunday night into Monday with winds easing and seas subsiding back below 10 feet.  Another frontal system will shift southward into area waters on Wednesday.

sections.synopsis: Gentle to moderate trade winds are expected through the weekend. Brief passing showers will drift into the islands on the northeasterly trade winds, favoring windward and mountain areas during the overnight to early morning hours. A more significant change to our weather pattern continues to evolve for next week. Deep tropical moisture moving across the state will bring the potential for heavy rain and thunderstorms to most islands starting around Tuesday and persisting through at least Thursday.
sections.prev_discussion:
Issued at 351 PM HST Fri Oct 23 2026 A surface trough just east of the state is visible on satellite imagery this afternoon, with peripheral clouds and showers tracking into east-facing slopes of the Big Island. This feature will maintain enhanced cloud cover and isolated to scattered showers across windward Big Island and Maui through tonight, before drifting eastward and pulling its deeper moisture away from the state.

Across the broader region, the surface pressure gradient remains relaxed as a broad low to the north splits two highs, one anchored to its east and the other to its west. Consequently, light to moderate trades will persist through Monday, allowing a hybrid trade wind and localized land/sea breeze pattern to take hold. A relatively dry air mass will keep skies mostly sunny to partly cloudy over the smaller islands through this evening, with only isolated windward showers moving in on the northeasterly flow. Meanwhile, high-level cirrus will continue streaming overhead from the west-southwest within a strong subtropical jet streak. Remnants of a dissipating frontal boundary trailing from the northern low as it dips southeastward will brush the western islands Saturday into Saturday night, providing a minor boost to the northeasterly trade wind speeds and windward showers across Kauai and Oahu.

Farther west, a low will attempt to organize near 15N and the Dateline this weekend. The National Hurricane Center currently assigns this feature a low (20 percent) chance of developing into a tropical cyclone over the next 7 days. Regardless of tropical development, the primary concern for Hawaii is an increasing risk of heavy rainfall leading to flash flooding, and isolated thunderstorms next week. This developing low and a large convergent band of deep tropical moisture to its east are expected to get swept up by a passing mid- to upper-level trough and drawn across the island chain. Global models continue to depict precipitable water (PW) values exceeding 2.5 inches over portions of the state late Tuesday through Wednesday, aligning with the strongest upper- level jet support for ascent. However, significant forecast uncertainty remains regarding exact timing, rainfall amounts, and which locations will experience the heaviest totals. Current guidance leans toward heavy rain arriving as early as Tuesday and potentially lingering through Thursday. While large-scale winds are nott expected to be hazardous, gusty winds may be possible within these heavy showers or in any thunderstorms that may develop.
sections.marine:
Issued at 351 PM HST Fri Oct 23 2026 A surface low centered about 1000 nm north of islands will move to the southeast through Saturday and will stall roughly 800 to 900 nm northeast of Oahu late Saturday through Monday, keeping the subtropical ridge just north of the area rather weak. Trade winds will be at gentle to moderate strength during much of this time, though a brief period of fresh northeast winds may accompany a shallow band of showers moving over Kauai and Oahu late Saturday. An area of low pressure is expected to move over the islands from the southwest Tuesday and Wednesday, bringing variable winds and the potential for heavy showers and thunderstorms.

Small surf will persist along north shores through early Saturday. A moderate, medium-period north-northwest swell will build late Saturday and produce surf around seasonal average during its peak on Sunday. As this swell declines on Monday, a long-period northwest swell will arrive. This swell will generate moderate surf along north- and west-facing shores through Wednesday. A small north- northeast swell will be possible during the second half of next week.

Small background level surf will prevail along south-facing shores into early Saturday. A series of small overlapping south- southwest swells will push surf back to around seasonal average late Saturday into early next week. A larger south-southwest swell is possible Thursday and next Friday.

Along east-facing shores, wind swell energy will be low through much of the week, but a small medium-period northeast swell will maintain small surf through tonight. Surf along most east facing shores will be small through early next week, but areas exposed to wrapping northerly swells will experience periods of moderate surf late Saturday through Monday and again during the second half of next week.
